title: Therapeutic observation and engagement
blurb: Choose and carry out the right level of observation as engagement, not watching, using NICE NG10 and NG225.
question: Priya, 23, was admitted after a serious overdose and says she still wants to die. The team places her on continuous observation. A healthcare assistant sits outside her open door reading a magazine. What should the nurse in charge do?

teach.body: Observation means knowing where a person is and how they are, at a level matched to their risk, while actively engaging with them. NICE NG10 covers it within restrictive interventions: it is used after positive engagement alone has not reduced the risk, and at the least intrusive level necessary. In plain English: it is time spent with someone to keep them safe and help them feel valued, not a guard watching a door.

head: Level
Frequency or proximity
Typical use
rows: Eyesight or arm's length of 1 nurse
Eyesight of 2-3 staff, arm's length of 1
teach.caption: Use these definitions unless a local policy states otherwise; many trusts say 'general', 'intermittent', 'within eyesight', 'within arm's length'.

items: Engages positively and actively with the person.
Is briefed on their history, background, risks and needs.
Knows the ward, emergency procedures and environmental risks.
Is approachable, listens and conveys that the person is valued.

steps.label: Engage first
steps.sub: Observation used if engagement has not reduced risk (1.4.12)

steps.label: Choose least intrusive level
steps.sub: Mental state, medicines, risk, the person's view (1.4.14, 1.4.17)

steps.label: Explain to the person
steps.sub: Why, aims, likely length, what ends it (1.4.15)

steps.label: Record and inform
steps.sub: Reasons, reviewer and date; tell the doctor if above general (1.4.16-1.4.22)

steps.label: Review
steps.sub: MDT review if it lasts 1 week or more (1.4.10)

items.label: maximum continuous stint above general level

teach.body: Sitting outside with a magazine is neither safe nor therapeutic. The nurse in charge, Tom, briefs the healthcare assistant on Priya's risks, asks her to stay within eyesight and engage with Priya, and plans a break before 2 hours. He explains to Priya why she is being observed, what it aims to do and what would allow it to be reduced, and asks how it feels for her. At handover Priya is included in the discussion. Untrained staff are not used (NG225 1.12.2).

teach.text: A shape under the covers is not an observation. The purpose is to confirm the person is safe, so at night the observer checks they are breathing and positioned safely, going in if unsure (in seclusion the Code says to assess consciousness and respirations of someone who appears asleep, 26.125).

teach.caption: NG10 1.4.13: people can find observation provocative and isolating; engagement reduces this.

items: Four NG10 levels: low intermittent (30-60 min), high intermittent (15-30 min), continuous, multiprofessional continuous.
Use the least intrusive level; explain why, the aims and what will end it.
Observers engage positively, are briefed and trained; untrained staff do not observe after self-harm.
No more than 2 hours of continuous above-general observation without a break.
Include the person in handover; tell the doctor when observation goes above general level.

summary: You can now match NG10 observation levels to risk, explain them to the person and carry them out as positive engagement. You can also apply the safeguards on breaks, handover, training, recording and review.

A.q: Under NICE NG10, how often is a patient checked on low-level intermittent observation?
options: Every 5-10 minutes
Every 15-30 minutes
Every 30-60 minutes
Every 2-4 hours
A.why: NG10 1.4.11: low-level intermittent observation is the baseline, once every 30 to 60 minutes.

whyNot.0: This is not an NG10 level; close risk is managed with continuous observation.
whyNot.1: Every 15-30 minutes is high-level intermittent observation.
whyNot.3: This is longer than the NG10 baseline interval.

A.q: What is the longest continuous period one staff member should spend on above-general observation without a break (NICE NG10)?
options: 1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
A full shift
A.why: NG10 1.4.20: an individual should not undertake a continuous period of observation above the general level for longer than 2 hours.

whyNot.0: One hour is shorter than the NG10 limit; breaks are needed by 2 hours.
whyNot.2: Four hours exceeds the NG10 limit and risks loss of concentration.
whyNot.3: A full shift without a break is unsafe and contrary to NG10.

A.q: Which description matches continuous observation in NICE NG10?
options: Within eyesight or arm's length of a designated nurse
Checked by any available staff member every 15 minutes
Within eyesight of 2 to 3 staff members
Located on the ward at each hourly check
A.why: NG10 1.4.11: continuous observation keeps the person within eyesight or at arm's length of a designated one-to-one nurse.

whyNot.1: Fifteen-minute checks are high-level intermittent observation.
whyNot.2: Eyesight of 2-3 staff is multiprofessional continuous observation.
whyNot.3: Hourly location checks are low-level intermittent observation.

B.q: Daniel, 30, is placed on high-level intermittent observation and asks the nurse why. Which explanation best follows NICE NG10?
options: That the doctor ordered it and it is ward policy
That it will continue until his discharge date
Why, its aims, how long and what will end it
That staff cannot discuss risk decisions with him
B.why: NG10 1.4.15: give information about why the person is under observation, its aims, how long it is likely to last and what needs to be achieved for it to stop.

whyNot.0: Citing policy without reasons does not meet the NG10 duty to explain.
whyNot.1: Observation is reviewed against risk, not fixed to discharge.
whyNot.3: Involving the person in decisions is required, not withheld.

B.q: The night nurse is handing over Asha's continuous observation to the day nurse. How should this be done according to NICE NG10?
options: Including Asha in the discussion where possible
In the office, away from Asha
In writing, so the observer can stay focused
After Asha has gone to breakfast
B.why: NG10 1.4.21: when handing over during a period of observation, include the service user in the discussion if possible.

whyNot.1: Leaving Asha unobserved for an office handover breaks continuous observation and excludes her.
whyNot.2: A written handover alone excludes Asha from the discussion.
whyNot.3: Delaying until she leaves removes her from the conversation and creates a gap.

B.q: On a general medical ward, the team wants close observation for Ms Okoye, 19, after self-harm. Who should observe her, according to NICE NG225?
options: The hospital security officer
A first-year student nurse on placement
Staff trained in clinical observation
Any healthcare assistant who is free
B.why: NG225 1.12.2: do not use staff untrained in clinical observation, such as security staff or trainees, to observe a person who has self-harmed; 1.14.4 requires training in engagement and rapport.

whyNot.0: Security staff are named in NG225 as untrained in clinical observation.
whyNot.1: Trainee staff are named as unsuitable for this observation.
whyNot.3: Availability is not the test; training in therapeutic observation is.

C.q: At 02:30, a nurse doing 15-minute observations looks into Callum's room. He is lying still with the duvet over his head. He has a history of ligature use. What should she do?
options: Record him as asleep and return in 15 minutes
Check from the door at the next round
Make sure he is breathing and safe, going in if unsure
Wake him fully at every check to confirm he is safe
C.why: Observation exists to confirm safety. A covered, still shape does not show he is breathing or free of a ligature, so the nurse checks breathing and position, entering the room if she cannot be sure (compare COP15 26.125).

whyNot.0: Recording 'asleep' without seeing he is safe defeats the purpose of observation.
whyNot.1: Waiting for the next round leaves a possible emergency unchecked.
whyNot.3: Waking him every time is unnecessarily intrusive; the aim is to confirm safety with least intrusion.

C.q: The nurse in charge raises Kofi's observation from low-level intermittent to continuous at 23:00. Which action is required by NICE NG10?
options: Inform his nearest relative by the next morning
Tell his psychiatrist or on-call doctor promptly
Arrange a Mental Health Act assessment tonight
Move him to a seclusion room overnight
C.why: NG10 1.4.22: tell the service user's psychiatrist or on-call doctor as soon as possible if observation above the general level is carried out.

whyNot.0: Carers may be told with his agreement, but the required step is informing the doctor.
whyNot.2: A change in observation level does not itself require an MHA assessment.
whyNot.3: Seclusion is a separate restrictive intervention, not a consequence of raised observation.

C.q: Rosa, 34, has been on continuous observation for 8 days. She says it makes her feel like a prisoner. What does NICE NG10 recommend now?
options: A multidisciplinary review of her observation
Continue unchanged until she stops complaining
Reduce it to low-level at once at her request
Transfer her to a psychiatric intensive care unit
C.why: NG10 1.4.10 and 1.4.13-1.4.17: observation lasting 1 week or more needs multidisciplinary review, taking account of the person's experience and views.

whyNot.1: Her experience must be taken into account, not dismissed.
whyNot.2: Her view matters, but the level is set by reviewing risk, not changed on request alone.
whyNot.3: Transfer is not indicated by the length of observation or her feelings.

reteach.title: Engage, don't just watch
reteach.question: What turns observation into therapeutic observation?

blocks.h: Time with a person, at the right distance
blocks.body: Pick the least intrusive NG10 level that keeps the person safe, explain it to them, and then use the time to engage: talk, listen, do something together. The observer must be trained and briefed, needs a break by 2 hours, and the plan is reviewed, with the person's view recorded.

blocks.text: Observation that does not confirm the person is breathing and safe is not observation.

explain.body: NG10 defines low-level intermittent (30-60 min), high-level intermittent (15-30 min), continuous (eyesight or arm's length of a designated nurse) and multiprofessional continuous (eyesight of 2-3 staff, arm's length of 1).

test.q: Which NG10 level is used when a person is at the highest risk of harming themselves or others?
options: High-level intermittent observation
Continuous observation by one nurse
Low-level intermittent observation
Multiprofessional continuous observation
test.why: NG10 1.4.11: multiprofessional continuous observation is for the highest risk, within eyesight of 2 or 3 staff and arm's length of at least 1.

whyNot.0: High-level intermittent is for risk that is not immediate.
whyNot.1: Continuous one-to-one is for an immediate threat, below the highest level.

explain.body: Choose the least intrusive level, balancing safety with dignity and privacy. Take account of mental state, medicines, risk and the person's views, and explain the reasons, aims, likely length and what will end it.

test.q: When deciding an observation level, which does NICE NG10 list as a factor to take into account?
options: The number of staff on the next shift
The person's prescribed and other medicines
The ward's average length of stay
How many other patients are on observation
test.why: NG10 1.4.17: consider current mental state, prescribed and non-prescribed medicines and their effects, the current risk assessment and the person's views.

whyNot.0: Staffing does not set the clinically required level.
whyNot.2: Average length of stay is not a clinical factor for this person.
whyNot.3: Other patients' observation levels do not determine this person's need.

explain.body: Observers take an active role in engaging positively, are briefed on the person's history and risks, know the ward and emergency procedures, and are approachable. After self-harm, only staff trained in clinical observation should observe.

test.q: A student nurse on continuous observation sits by the door writing her reflective log. What should the mentor advise?
options: Keep writing, as eyesight contact is enough
Move further away to give more privacy
Lock the door so she can concentrate
Engage with the patient as part of observing
test.why: NG10 1.4.19: staff undertaking observation should take an active role in engaging positively with the service user.

whyNot.0: Eyesight contact alone is watching, not therapeutic observation.
whyNot.1: Moving away could break continuous observation.
whyNot.2: Locking a door is unlawful confinement and breaks observation.

explain.body: No continuous stint above the general level longer than 2 hours. Include the person in handover where possible. Record who reviews the level and when, tell the doctor about above-general observation, and hold an MDT review if it lasts a week or more.

test.q: After how long should observation trigger a multidisciplinary review under NICE NG10?
options: 24 hours or more
72 hours or more
28 days or more
1 week or more
test.why: NG10 1.4.10: the observation policy should include the need for multidisciplinary review when observation continues for 1 week or more.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is not the NG10 trigger for MDT review.
whyNot.1: 72 hours is not the NG10 trigger.
whyNot.2: 28 days is far longer than the NG10 one-week trigger.
